b: Many studies show that trying to recall information, even guessing wrongly, strengthens memory more than reading it again. It's called the testing effect, and it's why Inkling asks you a question before showing the answer.

q.p: Which helps you remember more?

rq.p: What is the testing effect?
o: Studying the night before works best

why: Retrieving a memory rebuilds and strengthens it.

t: Half of people miss the gorilla
b: In a 1999 experiment, people counted basketball passes in a video. A person in a gorilla suit walked through the scene, and about half the viewers didn't notice. Focused attention can make us blind to the unexpected.

q.p: What did many viewers miss in the basketball video?
o: A person in a gorilla suit

rq.p: What does the gorilla study show?
o: Focus can blind us to obvious things

why: This is called inattentional blindness.

b: Psychologist Robert Zajonc found people tend to prefer things simply because they've seen them before, even nonsense words or shapes. This 'mere exposure effect' is one reason adverts repeat so often.

q.p: What tends to happen when we see something repeatedly?

rq.p: What is this effect called?

why: Familiar things feel easier to process, which feels pleasant.

b: Given a list to remember, people best recall the first few items and the last few, while the middle blurs. This serial position effect shapes everything from shopping lists to which job candidate an interviewer remembers.

q.p: Which items in a list do people remember best?

rq.p: What is this pattern called?

why: Early items get rehearsed; late items are still fresh.

t: Onions make you cry with a gas
b: Cutting an onion breaks its cells, mixing chemicals that create a gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. When it reaches your eyes it irritates them, and they make tears to wash it away. Chilling the onion first slows the reaction.

q.p: Why do onions make you cry?

rq.p: What reduces onion tears?

why: Cold slows the chemical reaction that makes the gas.

b: Capsaicin, the active chemical in chillies, binds to the same nerve receptors that detect real heat. Your brain gets a 'burning' signal with no actual temperature change. Milk helps because its casein protein carries capsaicin away.

q.p: Does chilli actually raise the temperature in your mouth?

rq.p: Why does milk help with chilli burn?
o: Its casein protein carries capsaicin away

why: Capsaicin is oily, so water just spreads it around.

b: Menthol in mint activates the same receptors that sense cold, called TRPM8. That's why mint feels cool even at room temperature, and why menthol is used in some cooling creams.

q.p: Why does mint feel cold?

rq.p: Which chemical in mint causes the effect?

why: It's the mirror image of how chilli fakes heat.

b: Each popcorn kernel holds a little water inside a tough shell. Heated to about 180 °C, the water turns to steam and the pressure builds until the shell bursts. The starchy inside puffs into foam and sets.

q.p: What makes popcorn pop?

rq.p: Why do some kernels never pop?
o: Their shells leak or they're too dry

why: No sealed water, no pressure.

b: Yeast are tiny fungi that eat sugars in dough and give off carbon dioxide gas. Stretchy gluten traps the bubbles, so the dough rises. Baking kills the yeast and sets the bubbly structure.

q.p: What gas makes bread rise?

rq.p: What traps the gas bubbles in dough?

why: Kneading builds the gluten network.

t: Salt makes ice melt below zero
b: Salt dissolves into the thin film of water on ice and lowers the temperature at which it freezes. The salty water stays liquid at temperatures where pure water would freeze, so the ice melts. It stops working well below about −10 °C.

q.p: How does road salt melt ice?

rq.p: When does road salt become much less effective?

why: Salt gets in the way of water forming ice crystals.

b: Soap molecules have one end that loves water and another that loves fats and oils. The fat-loving ends wedge into the oily outer layer of many viruses and germs, breaking them apart, and the water washes them away.

q.p: How does soap destroy many viruses?
o: It breaks their fatty outer layer

rq.p: What do soap molecules' two ends like?

why: Twenty seconds of scrubbing gives soap time to work.

b: Stainless steel contains at least about 10.5% chromium. The chromium reacts with oxygen to form an invisible layer that protects the iron beneath from rust. If scratched, the layer quickly re-forms.

q.p: What stops stainless steel rusting?

rq.p: What happens if stainless steel gets scratched?

why: Chromium oxide is tough and self-repairing.

b: In the same room, a metal bench and a wooden one are the same temperature. Metal feels colder because it conducts heat away from your skin much faster. Your nerves sense heat loss, not temperature.

q.p: In the same room, a metal spoon and a wooden spoon are…

rq.p: Why does metal feel colder?
o: It draws heat from skin faster

why: Skin senses the rate of heat flow.

t: A vacuum flask stops heat three ways
b: A vacuum flask has two walls with a vacuum between them, so heat can't conduct or move by air currents. The walls are silvered to reflect radiated heat. James Dewar invented it in 1892 for keeping chemicals cold.

q.p: What's between the walls of a vacuum flask?

rq.p: What was the vacuum flask first invented for?

why: No matter between the walls means no conduction.

b: A traditional incandescent bulb turns only about 5% of its electricity into visible light; the rest becomes heat. LEDs make the same light using around 80 to 90% less energy.

q.p: How much of an old bulb's energy became light?

rq.p: How much less energy do LEDs typically use?

why: Incandescent bulbs glow by heating a wire white-hot.

b: When an electric car slows down, its motor can run in reverse as a generator, turning the car's motion back into electricity for the battery. This regenerative braking also saves wear on the brake pads.

q.p: What happens to an electric car's energy when it brakes?
o: Some goes back into the battery

rq.p: What does the motor become during regenerative braking?

why: Motors and generators are the same machine run in opposite directions.

t: Planes cruise high to save fuel
b: Airliners usually cruise around 10 to 12 km up. The air there is much thinner, so there's less drag, and jet engines run efficiently. It also puts them above most weather.

q.p: Why do airliners fly so high?

rq.p: About how high do airliners usually cruise?

why: Less air to push through means less fuel burned.

t: Plane windows are round for a reason
b: In 1954, two de Havilland Comet jets broke apart in flight. Investigators traced metal fatigue cracks to the sharp corners of a rectangular opening in the cabin roof, where stress concentrates. Rounded openings spread stress evenly, which is why airliner windows are rounded.

q.p: Why are airliner windows rounded?

rq.p: Which aircraft disasters led to round windows?

why: Repeated pressurisation stresses the cabin each flight.

t: That tiny hole in plane windows
b: Airliner windows have several layers. A tiny 'breather hole' in the middle pane lets air pressure equalise between layers, so the outer pane takes the main load. It also helps stop the window fogging up.

q.p: What is the tiny hole in a plane window for?

rq.p: Which pane takes the main pressure load?

why: The inner panes are backups.

b: A narrow channel called the Eustachian tube links your middle ear to the back of your throat. When outside pressure changes, swallowing or yawning opens it, letting air rush through to equalise pressure, which you feel as a pop.

q.p: What equalises pressure in your ears?

rq.p: What helps your ears pop on a plane?

why: Muscles that open the tube work when you swallow.

t: Lift safety brakes made skyscrapers possible
b: In 1854, Elisha Otis stood on a lift platform and had its only rope cut in front of a crowd in New York. His spring-loaded safety brake caught it. Safe lifts made tall buildings practical.

q.p: What did Elisha Otis do to show off his invention?

rq.p: Why did safe lifts matter?

why: Fear of falling had kept buildings short.

t: Ships float by pushing water aside
b: A steel ship floats because its hollow hull pushes aside a weight of water equal to its own weight before it sinks too far. This is Archimedes' principle. Squash the same steel into a solid lump and it would sink.

q.p: Why does a heavy steel ship float?

rq.p: Whose principle explains floating?

why: Shape matters: a hull displaces far more water than a lump.

b: Antibiotics attack features of bacteria, such as their cell walls. Viruses don't have those features, so antibiotics don't help with colds or flu. Using them unnecessarily helps bacteria evolve resistance.

q.p: Do antibiotics treat a common cold?

rq.p: What does overusing antibiotics cause?

why: Bacteria that survive the drug pass on their resistance.

t: Face unlock uses thousands of invisible dots
b: Apple's Face ID projects over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto your face and reads how they land, building a 3D map. That's why a flat photo can't fool it the way it fools simpler 2D camera systems.

q.p: Why can't a photo fool Face ID?

rq.p: What does Face ID project onto your face?

why: Depth information is hard to fake with a picture.

t: Toast often lands butter side down
b: Physicist Robert Matthews showed that a slice of toast sliding off a typical table only has time to make about half a rotation before landing. So if it starts butter side up, it tends to land butter side down.

q.p: Why does dropped toast often land butter side down?
o: Table height allows about half a turn

rq.p: What would help toast land butter side up?

why: Matthews won an Ig Nobel Prize for the study in 1996.
